title: Three-observable measurement of the critical velocity in a paraxial superfluid of light flowing past a mobile impurity
authors: T. Aladjidi, M. Baker-Rasooli, T. D. Ferreira, A. Bramati, M. Albert, Q. Glorieux, P. -É. Larré
abstract: We report the measurement of the critical velocity of a paraxial superfluid of light flowing past a mobile impurity, realized using a dual-wavelength optical scheme in a warm vapor of $^{87}\text{Rb}$. The superflow is two-dimensional by nature, while the impurity features a highly repulsive potential, a large tunable radius, and a finite mass. The critical velocity is evaluated by simultaneously monitoring three complementary observables: the number of vortices nucleated in the wake of the impurity, the hydrodynamic force exerted on it, and its displacement velocity relative to the flow. These independent methods yield consistent values for the critical velocity, which remain systematically below the Landau criterion and decrease with the impurity radius, in qualitative agreement with theoretical expectations. Our results demonstrate the reliability of these combined diagnostics, establishing paraxial superfluids of light as a versatile platform for exploring the impurity problem in quantum hydrodynamics.
summary: This research reports the measurement of the critical velocity in a superfluid of light flowing past an impurity using a sophisticated dual-wavelength optical setup. By independently measuring vortex nucleation, hydrodynamic force, and impurity displacement, the authors cross-validate the critical velocity threshold. This establishes the superfluid of light as a versatile and reliable platform for testing quantum hydrodynamic theories.
main_problem: The paper measures the critical velocity at which a paraxial superfluid of light transitions to a dissipative state when flowing past a mobile impurity.
main_result: The critical velocity was measured using three independent diagnostics (vortex count, hydrodynamic force, and impurity velocity), yielding consistent results that systematically fall below the Landau criterion.
method: The critical velocity is determined by monitoring the onset of energy dissipation, specifically through the nucleation of quantized vortices, while simultaneously measuring the force and displacement on the impurity.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D paraxial superfluid of light, modeled by the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, flowing past a highly repulsive, finite-mass impurity created optically in a warm vapor of Rb-87.
key_observables: Number of nucleated vortices, hydrodynamic force on the impurity, and the impurity's displacement velocity relative to the flow.
important_parameters: Mach number (v0/cs), impurity radius ($\sigma$), and the ratio $\sigma/\xi$ (impurity size to healing length).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the superfluid being governed by the NLS equation and assumes the three diagnostic methods provide a self-consistent benchmark for the critical transition.
figures_summary: Figures likely show the experimental setup and plots comparing the critical velocity ($ eta_c$) extracted from the three different measurement techniques as a function of the impurity radius ($\sigma/\xi$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (NLS equation for superfluid light), details the experimental setup using a dual-wavelength scheme, presents the three complementary measurement techniques, and concludes by cross-validating the results to establish a robust benchmark for the critical velocity.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled, optical platform to study fundamental quantum hydrodynamic phenomena, such as superfluid critical velocities and vortex dynamics, which are central topics in both quantum gas and quantum optics research.

The 2D paraxial superfluid of light (transverse slices on the sketch) is generated using a wide Gaussian laser beam (red) propagating through a warm 87Rb vapor (blue). The optical impurity at the center of the planar superfluid is created by injecting a narrower Gaussian beam (gray). The relative angle between the red beam and the axis along the rubidium cell controls the incident velocity of the superfluid past the impurity, which is on-axis when the fluid is at rest.
